stages.topic: How to Convert a PDF to Word Without Losing the Formatting
stages.brief:
I've finished the brief. The chosen query is **how to convert pdf to word**. The top results are mostly converter tools that don't explain much. The angle is to help readers pick the right method for their kind of PDF, using official notes on what converts badly. Each method links to its own vendor's documentation. Two gaps: I found no search-volume data, and I couldn't read three Adobe Help pages (details in section 7).

---

# CONTENT BRIEF: New Earns, PDF pillar

## 1. Chosen query and intent

- **Primary query:** how to convert pdf to word
- **Focus keyphrase:** convert PDF to Word. Use it in the title, the intro and once or twice more. Don't put it in every heading.
- **Working title:** How to Convert a PDF to Word Without Losing the Formatting: Pick the Right Method for Your File
- **Search intent:** a how-to with a task to get done. The reader has a PDF and wants an editable Word file now, with the layout kept.
- **What ranks now:** a search on "how to convert pdf to word" returned mostly converter tool pages: Drawboard, Microsoft's PDF-to-Word marketing page, Adobe's online converter, iLovePDF, Smallpdf and Nitro. A search for "without losing formatting" returned listicles from PDF-software vendors (PDFgear, Wondershare, PDNob, UPDF) that mainly push their own tool.
- **Search-demand data:** none was provided, and I haven't estimated any volumes.

## 2. Unique angle (the value we add)

Current results say "upload, click convert, done." None of them help readers choose a method based on what's in their PDF, and none use the vendors' own lists of what breaks. New Earns can add:

1. **A first check of the file type.** Is the PDF mostly text, mostly charts or graphics, or a scan/photo? Microsoft says the result depends on this (see facts M2–M4).
2. **Three methods with sourced steps.** (a) Microsoft Word on the desktop, (b) Google Drive/Docs, which is free and includes OCR, then download as .docx, (c) Adobe Acrobat (the free online tool, paid Acrobat, or Reader with an Export PDF subscription).
3. **A decision table:** PDF type → best method → what to expect.
4. **A "what will break" section** built on Microsoft's official list of elements that don't convert well, and Google's list of what OCR won't detect.
5. **Troubleshooting:** fixes for "the page came in as an image," "footnotes are in the body text," "tables or columns are gone," and "the file is too big for Google Drive."
6. **A privacy note for freelancers handling client files.** Online tools upload the file to a server. Adobe states what it does with uploaded files.

## 3. Outline (H2/H3)

**Intro (2–3 sentences).** You can convert a PDF to Word in the Word app you already have, for free in Google Drive, or with Acrobat. Whether the formatting survives depends mostly on what kind of PDF you have. Don't open with filler.

**H2: First, check what kind of PDF you have**
- H3: Mostly text (contracts, reports, invoices). Word handles these best (M2).
- H3: Mostly charts, graphics or designed layouts. A page may come through as an uneditable image (M3).
- H3: Scanned pages or photos of documents. These need text recognition (OCR) (G1, A4, R3).
- Practical tip, framed as general guidance and not as a sourced fact: try selecting a line of text in your PDF reader. If you can't, it's probably a scan or image.

**H2: Quick decision table: which method to use**
Columns: Your PDF | Best first try | What to expect | Source

| Your PDF | Best first try | What to expect | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mostly text | Word, File > Open | Close match; lines and page breaks may shift | M1, M2, M5 |
| Scanned or photo, small file | Google Drive > Open with Google Docs, then download .docx | Bold, italics, font size, font type and line breaks likely kept; lists, tables, columns and footnotes not likely detected | G1–G4 |
| Scanned or complex layout | Acrobat (online or paid) | Adobe says it rebuilds columns, tables, headers/footers and footnotes "in most cases"; OCR runs on scanned text | A1–A5 |
| Contains a known problem element (bookmarks, comments, tracked changes, etc.) | Consider not converting: open the PDF directly | Microsoft's own advice | M6 |

**H2: Method 1: Convert a PDF to Word in Microsoft Word**
- Steps M-steps 1–4 (File > Open > find the PDF > OK on the conversion message > save as Word doc or PDF).
- Note: Word converts a copy and leaves the original PDF alone (M1, M7).
- Note: page-to-page correspondence may not be exact (M5).
- Versions: Microsoft's pages list Word for Microsoft 365, Word 2024, 2021, 2019 and 2016. Say menus may look slightly different between versions.

**H2: Method 2: Use Google Drive and Google Docs (free, with OCR)**
- Prepare the file: the 2 MB size guideline, text at least 10 pixels high, pages right way up, common fonts, sharp images (G1).
- Convert: right-click the file in Drive > Open with Google Docs (G2).
- Get a Word file: File > Download > choose a file type (G5). Tell the reader to pick Microsoft Word (.docx). Google's page says "Choose a file type" and doesn't name .docx, so the writer should say the menu lists the formats.
- What survives and what doesn't (G3, G4).

**H2: Method 3: Use Adobe Acrobat (online, desktop or Reader)**
- H3: Acrobat's free online converter: steps, sign-in, free-use limits, file handling (A1–A3, F1–F4).
- H3: Acrobat desktop: Export PDF > Microsoft Word > Word Document > Export; OCR runs automatically on scanned text (A4). Say the tool's location in the interface may differ by Acrobat version. This page is Adobe marketing, not a help page.
- H3: Acrobat Reader: you need a paid Adobe Acrobat Export PDF subscription. Steps are All Tools > Export a PDF. For scans, set Document Language (R1–R3).
- Formats: .docx and .doc, plus RTF (A6).

**H2: What usually breaks, and how to fix it**
- The full Microsoft list (M6).
- Why it happens: PDF is a fixed format that usually doesn't store paragraphs, tables or columns (M8). One short paragraph in plain English.
- Fixes, each tied to a source:
  - The whole page is an image or the text won't edit → try an OCR route (Google Drive or Acrobat) (M3, G2, A4).
  - The footnote ended up in the body → Word didn't recognise it; reinsert it by hand (M4).
  - Tables, lists or columns are flattened after Google OCR → expected (G4); use Word or Acrobat for table-heavy files.
  - Google Drive won't convert it well and the file is big → the guideline is 2 MB or smaller (G1). Internal link: compress or split the file first.
  - The PDF has comments, bookmarks or tracked changes → these don't convert well; keep the PDF for reference (M6).

**H2: Converting client documents? Check where the file goes**
- Online converters upload the file. Adobe says the file is handled on its servers and deleted unless you sign in to save it (A2, F4). It also says it uses AES-256 and TLS 1.2 (F3).
- Word desktop converts a copy of the file you opened (M1). Don't add privacy claims about Word beyond that.
- **Optional product mention** (see section 6).

**H2: FAQ (short)**
- Is there a free way? Yes: Google Drive (G2, G5), Word if you already have it, or Adobe's online tool within its free limits (F1, F2).
- Can I convert a scanned PDF? Yes, with OCR (G1–G2, A4, A5).
- Why do the line or page breaks differ? (M5)

## 4. Facts to rely on (with URLs)

**Microsoft: "Edit a PDF"**: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/word/training/edit-a-pdf (the old /office/edit-a-pdf-b2d1d729… URL redirects here; cite this one)
- M1: Steps: File > Open; find and open the PDF; Word says it will make a copy and convert it, and the original PDF won't be changed; select OK; save as a Word doc or PDF from the Save as dropdown.
- M2 (also on page M-b): works best with PDFs that are mostly text.
- M5: the converted document may not match the original page for page.

**Microsoft: "Opening PDFs in Word"**: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/word/opening-pdfs-in-word
- M2: works best with mostly-text files (business, legal, scientific).
- M3: a mostly-chart/graphics PDF may come in as a whole-page image whose text can't be edited.
- M4: an unrecognised footnote becomes regular text.
- M6: list of elements that don't convert well.
- M7: you always keep the original PDF.
- M8: how conversion works (fixed format, no structure).

**Google Drive Help: "Convert PDF and photo files to text"**: https://support.google.com/drive/answer/176692
- G1: preparation tips (formats, 2 MB, 10 px text, orientation, fonts, image quality).
- G2: steps (right-click > Open with Google Docs).
- G3: likely kept: bold, italics, font size, font type, line breaks.
- G4: not likely detected: lists, tables, columns, footnotes, endnotes.

**Google Docs Editors Help: "Create, view, or download a file"**: https://support.google.com/docs/answer/49114?hl=en&co=GENIE.Platform%3DDesktop
- G5: File > Download > choose a file type.

**Adobe: online PDF to Word converter**: https://www.adobe.com/acrobat/online/pdf-to-word.html
- A1: steps.
- A2: file handling.
- A3: you may be asked to sign in on repeat use.
- A5: OCR and accuracy claim (vendor's own wording, so attribute it to Adobe).
- A6: .docx, .doc and RTF.

**Adobe: "How to convert a PDF to Word"** (marketing how-to): https://www.adobe.com/acrobat/how-to/pdf-to-word-doc-converter.html
- A4: desktop Export PDF steps; text recognition runs automatically on scanned text.

**Adobe Help: "FAQ | Try Adobe Acrobat online services"**: https://helpx.adobe.com/document-cloud/faq/try-acrobat-online-services.html
- F1: without sign-in, one free transaction.
- F2: signed in, one free premium-tool transaction every 30 days, rolling.
- F3: encryption.
- F4: deletion if you don't sign in.
- F5: PDF to Word output = DOCX.

**Adobe Help: "Export PDF from Acrobat Reader"**: https://helpx.adobe.com/reader/desktop/export-pdf.html
- R1: paid subscription needed.
- R2: steps.
- R3: set Document Language for scans.

**Don't state these (no source read):** Word for the web or Word for Mac opening PDFs; any prices; Adobe file-size or page limits; Google Docs keeping images; the "Retain flowing text vs page layout" settings in Acrobat.

## 5. Internal-link ideas (only those genuinely related)

- **"How to Compress a PDF for Email (and What to Do When It's Still Too Big)"**: link in the troubleshooting item about Google Drive's 2 MB guideline.
- **"How to Password-Protect a PDF (and What the Password Doesn't Protect)"**: link where the reader edits the Word file and saves it back to PDF to send to a client. Don't claim that protected PDFs fail to convert; I have no source for that.
- None of the other published articles match this intent. Don't force links.

## 6. Product link: justified, at most twice, with care

- **Where it fits:** Method 3 or the client-files section, as another browser-based option for PDF-to-Word. It's also justified in the scanned-PDF troubleshooting item through its image-to-text tool. Don't exceed two mentions.
- **Allowed wording:** Private PDF Editor (https://private-pdf-editor.com/) is a browser-based PDF toolkit with about 30 tools. It converts PDF to Word, PowerPoint, Excel, JPG and PDF/A, and it also offers image to text. Standard PDF editing runs in the browser, but some conversions are handled differently and have separate disclosures, so check its disclosure for PDF-to-Word before uploading client files. It has paid plans (see its pricing page for current prices).
- **Don't say:** that PDF-to-Word runs locally or privately, anything about its formatting accuracy, or any price. Don't compare it to Adobe, Google or Microsoft.

## 7. Notes for the writer

- No first-hand testing language ("we tried," "in our test").
- Menus change. Add a line that menu names may differ by version and platform, especially for Acrobat. The Acrobat desktop steps come from Adobe's marketing page. I couldn't read Adobe's desktop Help pages: the PDF-to-Word page returned an HTML-conversion page, and the Acrobat-web "Export PDFs" and "Recognize text" pages returned no readable body text. Don't add Acrobat settings beyond what's quoted here.
- The Adobe free-limit FAQ says "Last updated on Jun 2, 2025." Present the limits as "Adobe's FAQ says…" and tell readers they'll be told online when they hit a limit.

article.title: How to Convert PDF to Word Without Losing the Formatting: Pick the Right Method for Your File
article.seo_title: How to Convert PDF to Word Without Losing Formatting
article.meta_description: Convert PDF to Word with Microsoft Word, Google Docs or Adobe Acrobat. See which method suits text, scanned or complex PDFs, and what formatting breaks.
article.excerpt: You can convert PDF to Word in Microsoft Word, in Google Drive and Docs, or with Adobe Acrobat. Whether the formatting survives depends mostly on what kind of PDF you have. Here is how to check your file, pick a method, and fix what breaks.
article.content_html:
You have a PDF and need an editable Word file. You can convert PDF to Word in the Word app you may already have, through Google Drive and Google Docs, or with Adobe Acrobat. Whether the layout survives depends mostly on what kind of PDF you start with. This guide starts there, then covers each method using the vendors' own documentation.

First, check what kind of PDF you have

Microsoft's support page on opening PDFs in Word says conversion "works best with files that are mostly text" and warns that the result "might not look exactly the way it looked as a PDF." Before you pick a method, decide which of these three groups your file belongs to.

Mostly text (contracts, reports, invoices)

Microsoft says files that are mostly text, such as business, legal or scientific documents, convert best (Microsoft Support). Its Edit a PDF guide adds a warning: PDFs of book chapters, or "something that looks like a manuscript from a copier," won't be formatted well in Word.

Mostly charts, graphics or designed layouts

If the PDF contains mostly charts or other graphics, Microsoft says the whole page might show up as an image, and the text on it can't be edited (Microsoft Support). If your file is a heavily designed layout, such as slides saved as a PDF, plan for this and keep a text-recognition (OCR) method in reserve.

Scanned pages or photos of documents

A scan is a picture of text. To make it editable, the text must first be recognised with optical character recognition (OCR). Google Drive can convert PDF and photo files to text when you open them with Google Docs (Google Drive Help). Adobe says Acrobat runs text recognition automatically on scanned text when you export to Word (Adobe). Adobe's Reader help also tells you to set the Document Language when you export a scanned document or image (Adobe Help).

Here is a quick check that works in most PDF readers. Try to highlight a single line of text with your cursor. If you can select individual words, the PDF has a text layer. If the whole page selects as one block, or nothing selects at all, the file is probably a scan or an image. In that case, go straight to a method that includes OCR.

Quick decision table: which method to use

Your PDFBest first tryWhat to expectSource
Mostly textMicrosoft Word: File > OpenA close match, but lines and pages may break in different placesMicrosoft: Edit a PDF
Scanned or photo, small fileGoogle Drive: Open with Google Docs, then download as WordBold, italics, font size, font type and line breaks are likely kept. Lists, tables, columns, footnotes and endnotes are not likely to be detected.Google Drive Help
Scanned or complex layoutAdobe Acrobat (online tool or desktop)Adobe says it reconstructs multi-column layouts, tables, headers and footers, and footnotes "in most cases." OCR may be used for scanned text.Adobe
Contains bookmarks, comments, tracked changes or other elements that don't convert wellConsider not converting: open the PDF directlyMicrosoft suggests opening such files directly rather than converting themMicrosoft: Opening PDFs in Word

Method 1: Convert a PDF to Word in Microsoft Word

Microsoft's instructions apply to Word for Microsoft 365, Word 2024, Word 2021, Word 2019 and Word 2016 (Microsoft Support). Menus may look slightly different between versions.

  1. In Word, go to File > Open.
  2. Find the PDF and open it. You might have to select Browse and look for the PDF in a folder.
  3. Word tells you it will make a copy of the PDF and convert its contents into a format Word can display. The original PDF won't be changed. Select OK.
  4. Make your edits. Then save the file as a Word document or a PDF: in the Save menu, choose the document type from the Save as dropdown and select OK.

These steps come from Microsoft's Edit a PDF guide. Two points from Microsoft are worth knowing before you start:

  • Your original is safe. Word converts a copy. Microsoft says "you always have the original PDF file, in case you don't want to keep the version that Word converts" (Microsoft Support).
  • Pages may not line up exactly. The converted document "might not have a perfect page-to-page correspondence with the original." Lines and pages may break in different places (Microsoft Support).

If you are editing a client document and saving it back to PDF to send, you may also want to restrict who can open it. See How to Password-Protect a PDF (and What the Password Doesn't Protect).

Method 2: Use Google Drive and Google Docs (includes OCR)

This route suits scanned PDFs and photos of documents, because Google Docs recognises the text as it converts. It takes three steps: prepare the file, convert it, then download it as a Word file.

Prepare the file

Google lists these tips "for the best results" (Google Drive Help):

  • Format: PDFs (multipage documents) or photo files (.jpeg, .png and .gif).
  • File size: Google recommends 2 MB or smaller.
  • Resolution: text should be at least 10 pixels high.
  • Orientation: pages must be right side up.
  • Language: Google Drive detects the language of the document.
  • Fonts: use common fonts, such as Arial or Times New Roman.
  • Image quality: use sharp images with even lighting and clear contrast.

These are recommendations, not hard limits. A larger or blurrier file may still convert, but the results are likely to be worse.

Convert it

  1. On your computer, go to Google Drive and upload the PDF if it isn't there already.
  2. Right-click the file.
  3. Click Open with Google Docs.

Steps from Google Drive Help.

Download it as a Word file

  1. With the converted document open in Google Docs, click File > Download at the top.
  2. Choose a file type. The menu lists the available formats; pick Microsoft Word (.docx).
  3. The file downloads to your computer.

Steps from Google Docs Editors Help.

What survives and what doesn't

Google says the format "might not transfer" in full. Bold, italics, font size, font type and line breaks are likely to be kept. Lists, tables, columns, footnotes and endnotes are not likely to be detected (Google Drive Help). This route works well for getting the words out of a scan. It is a weaker choice for table-heavy or multi-column documents.

Method 3: Use Adobe Acrobat (online, desktop or Reader)

Adobe offers three ways to do this. Menu names and tool locations may differ between Acrobat versions and platforms, so treat the paths below as a guide.

Acrobat's free online converter

  1. Go to Adobe's online PDF to Word converter.
  2. Click Select a file, or drag and drop the file into the drop zone.
  3. Select the PDF you want to convert. Acrobat converts it to an editable Word document (DOCX).
  4. Download your file. If you use the tool again, you may be asked to sign in to download it.

Adobe says the tool works on Mac, Windows, iOS, Android and Linux. It also says Acrobat "identifies and reconstructs multi-column layouts, embedded tables, headers and footers, and footnotes in most cases," and that its built-in OCR may be used on complex scanned PDFs (Adobe). That is Adobe's own description of its tool, so expect to check the result.

On free use, Adobe's FAQ (last updated June 2, 2025) says that without signing in, most tools let you complete one free transaction and download the result one time. Signed-in users trying premium tools such as Convert PDF to Word get one free transaction every 30 days on a rolling basis. Adobe says you'll be notified online when you reach the free limits (Adobe Help).

Acrobat desktop

Adobe's how-to page gives these steps (Adobe):

  1. Open the PDF in Acrobat.
  2. Click the Export PDF tool. Adobe's page places it in the right pane, but newer layouts may put it somewhere else.
  3. Choose Microsoft Word as your export format, then Word Document.
  4. Click Export. If the PDF contains scanned text, Adobe says Acrobat runs text recognition automatically.
  5. Name the file, choose DOC or DOCX, and click Save.

On format choice, Adobe says Acrobat can export to both .docx and .doc and recommends .docx on modern systems. You can also export to RTF (Rich Text Format) (Adobe).

Acrobat Reader

The free Reader app can export to Word only if you have a paid subscription to the Adobe Acrobat Export PDF service (Adobe Help). With that subscription in place:

  1. Click Sign In in the upper-right corner of the Reader window and sign in with your Adobe ID.
  2. Select All Tools > Export a PDF. The open file is selected for conversion by default.
  3. From the Export PDF To list, choose the Word format.
  4. Select Convert to the chosen format.
  5. In the Save as dialog, choose a location and select Save.

For a scanned document or image, make sure the Document Language matches the text in the file. To change it, click Change and choose the language from the list (Adobe Help).

What usually breaks, and how to fix it

Microsoft publishes a list of document elements that don't convert well. If your PDF includes these, it suggests you "might want to open it directly rather than converting it to a Word document" (Microsoft Support):

  • Tables with cell spacing
  • Page colors and page borders
  • Tracked changes
  • Frames
  • Footnotes that span more than one page
  • Endnotes
  • Audio, video and PDF active elements
  • PDF bookmarks
  • PDF tags
  • PDF comments
  • Font effects such as Glow or Shadow, which appear as graphics in the Word file

Why does this happen? Microsoft explains that PDF is a fixed file format. Most PDFs don't store information about paragraphs, tables or columns. A table, for example, is stored as a set of lines with no link to the content in its cells. Word applies a set of rules to guess which headings, lists and tables best match the original (Microsoft Support). When the guess is wrong, the layout shifts.

Here are fixes for the most common problems:

  • The page came in as an image and the text won't edit. Microsoft says this can happen with PDFs that are mostly charts or graphics (Microsoft Support). Try a route with text recognition instead: Google Drive's Open with Google Docs (Google Drive Help), or Acrobat's Export PDF, which Adobe says runs text recognition on scanned text (Adobe).
  • A footnote ended up in the body text. If Word doesn't recognise a footnote, it treats it as regular text and might not put it at the bottom of the page (Microsoft Support). Cut the text and reinsert it as a footnote by hand.
  • Tables, lists or columns are flattened after Google conversion. This is expected: Google says these are not likely to be detected (Google Drive Help). For table-heavy files, try Word or Acrobat instead.
  • The file is large and Google Drive doesn't convert it well. Google recommends files of 2 MB or smaller (Google Drive Help). Shrink the file first, or split off just the pages you need. Our guide How to Compress a PDF for Email (and What to Do When It's Still Too Big) covers both.
  • Images look blurry in the Word file. Adobe says image resolution is kept at the level stored in the original PDF. If the images look low-resolution, the original PDF may already have contained reduced-resolution images (Adobe). In that case, ask for the original image files.
  • The PDF has comments, bookmarks or tracked changes. These are on Microsoft's list of elements that don't convert well (Microsoft Support). Keep the PDF open alongside the Word file for reference.

Converting client documents? Check where the file goes

If you freelance, the PDF may be a client's contract, financial report or unpublished work. Before you convert it, know where the file is sent.

  • Online converters upload your file. Adobe's converter page says your file "will be securely handled by Adobe servers and deleted unless you sign in to save it" (Adobe). Adobe's FAQ says that if you don't sign in to save or share the file, Adobe deletes it from the server "within a short time period." It also says Acrobat online services use AES-256 encryption and TLS 1.2, and that uploaded files stored in Adobe cloud storage are automatically labelled Private (Adobe Help).
  • Word desktop converts a copy of the file you opened. Microsoft says Word makes a copy and leaves the original PDF unchanged (Microsoft Support).
  • Google Drive needs the file in your Drive. The conversion starts from a file stored in Google Drive (Google Drive Help), so check whether your client agreement allows that.

If you prefer a browser-based toolkit, Private PDF Editor includes a PDF to Word converter among its roughly 30 tools. Standard PDF editing runs in the browser, but some conversions are handled differently and have separate disclosures. Read its PDF to Word disclosure before you upload a client file. It has paid plans; see its pricing page for current prices.

Disclosure: Private PDF Editor is built by the team behind New Earns. We mention it where it fits the task; the steps in this guide also work with other tools.

FAQ

Is there a free way to convert PDF to Word?

There are options that don't require buying a converter. In Google Drive, you can open the file with Google Docs and then use File > Download to save it as a Word file (Google Drive Help, Google Docs Editors Help). If you already have Word, it can open and convert PDFs (Microsoft Support). Adobe's online tool also allows limited free transactions; its FAQ describes one free transaction without signing in, and one every 30 days for signed-in users trying premium tools (Adobe Help).

Can I convert a scanned PDF to Word?

Yes, but you need a method that recognises text. Google Drive converts PDF and photo files to text when you open them with Google Docs, and works best with sharp, right-side-up pages and files of 2 MB or smaller (Google Drive Help). Adobe says Acrobat runs text recognition automatically on scanned text during export (Adobe). If you only have photos of document pages, Private PDF Editor also offers an image to text tool.

Why do line and page breaks differ from the original?

Microsoft says the converted document might not match the original page for page, and lines and pages may break in different places (Microsoft Support). This happens because most PDFs don't store structure such as paragraphs, tables or columns, so Word has to rebuild the layout from rules (Microsoft Support). Expect to tidy up breaks by hand, especially before you send the file to a client.
